The quote was re-fetched on 2026-09-23 and FOUND verbatim on the NBER page. The authors and working-paper number match the NBER citation.

The label misstates what was measured. 'Adopted' in the abstract means weekly active users. The paper's body says: 'By the end of July 2025, ChatGPT had more than 700 million total WAU, nearly 10% of the world’s adult population.' Footnote 20 adds that the counts are of accounts (login credentials or browser cookies), which 'somewhat exceed distinct people'. The measure covers consumer plans (Free, Plus, Pro) only. The label should say weekly users, so it is not confused with Pew's 'ever used' measure.

The notes understate the company affiliation. They say the NBER page discloses that 'an author' is an OpenAI employee. In fact two authors disclose it on the NBER page: Aaron Chatterji ('I am an employee of OpenAI and this paper was written as part of my responsibilities there') and Zoe Hitzig ('I am a full-time employee of OpenAI'). The paper itself lists an OpenAI affiliation for six of the seven authors; all except David Deming.
The source date is imprecise. The NBER page shows 'Issue Date: September 2025' (datetime 2025-09-12), and the paper PDF is dated September 15, 2025.
'Rather than human readers' is supported by the paper ('without any human ever reading the contents of a message'), but not by the NBER abstract alone. I added the paper PDF as a source.

fieldFixes.label: Weekly ChatGPT users as a share of the world's adult population, July 2025
fieldFixes.notes: About 700 million weekly active users on ChatGPT's consumer plans (Free, Plus, Pro) by the end of July 2025. The paper calls this 'nearly 10%' of the world's adult population, and the abstract 'around 10%'. It counts accounts, which the authors say somewhat exceed distinct people. This is not comparable with Pew's 'ever used' measure for U.S. adults. The research is company research: two authors (Aaron Chatterji and Zoe Hitzig) disclose on the NBER page that they are OpenAI employees, and six of the seven list an OpenAI affiliation in the paper. The paper classified a sample of conversations with an automated, privacy-preserving LLM pipeline 'without any human ever reading the contents of a message'. That method is itself an example of the data-use questions this study is about.

fieldFixes.notes: Announced 24 August 2022. The Attorney General alleged Sephora did not disclose that it sold personal information, did not process opt-outs sent via user-enabled global privacy controls, and did not cure within 30 days. The CCPA already required businesses to honour such signals. The settlement showed that ignoring a browser-sent, machine-readable preference carries a penalty, a direct precursor of person-proffered terms. The same day the AG sent notices to other businesses that failed to process such signals.
